      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">RA</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> (RA) is a form of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that causes pain, swelling, and stiffness in your joints. RA is an autoimmune disease. Although it is most common in the wrist and fingers, this disease can cause your immune system to attack any joint tissue. The inflammation (swelling) that comes with RA can also affect other body parts. Inflammation could cause medical issues in your eyes, skin, heart, nerves, blood, or lungs.</p><p>RA differs from <span class="qt0">osteoarthritis</span>, a common <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that often comes with age. RA affects the lining of your joints and damages the tissue that covers the ends of the bones in a joint. Eventually, this might cause your joints to not work as well.</p><p>There is no cure for RA, but early treatment can help you manage symptoms, reduce joint damage, and lead a productive life.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> can happen at any age, but your risk increases as you become an older adult. Your chance of developing RA can also increase if:</p><ul><li>You're a woman. Women are more likely to get RA than men.</li><li>You have a family history. If a member of your family has RA, you're more likely to get the disease.</li><li>You're a smoker.Smoking over a long period of time increases your risk of getting RA and how serious the disease can be.</li><li>You have other medical conditions that may increase your risk of getting RA. These include obesity, gum disease, and lung disease.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>No one knows what causes <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. A few things that might play a part in getting RA include:</p><ul><li>Your genes are parts of DNA in your cells that are passed down from your parents. Certain genes may increase your risk of getting <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>, but not everyone with these genes gets RA.</li><li>The environment, which includes things such as cigarette smoke, sometimes triggers RA symptoms.</li><li>Hormones are chemical messengers in your bloodstream that control the actions of certain cells or organs. Researchers think that sex hormones might play a role in getting RA. Women are more likely to develop the disease, and RA symptoms may change during and after pregnancy.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Your immune system may start turning against your body's joints and tissues years before you notice any symptoms of RA. The changes from this type of immune malfunction usually settle in your joints.</p><p>RA affects people differently. You might have the disease for only a short time, or your symptoms might come and go. The severe form can be chronic (long-lasting) and may last a lifetime.</p><p>Symptoms of <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> may include:</p><ul><li>Joint pain or stiffness when moving. This is usually worse in the morning or after inactivity. RA usually affects both joints. If one of your hands or knees is affected, so is the other.</li><li>Joint tenderness, redness, and warmth.</li><li>Joint swelling may make daily activities hard. These could include things such as combing your hair, buttoning your clothes, or bending your knees.</li><li>Fatigue, fever, and a loss of appetite.</li><li>Hard bumps (<span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> nodules) under your skin near the joints.</li></ul>How is <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> diagnosed?<p>There's no single test for <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. The disease develops over time. At first, you may only have a few symptoms, making it hard to diagnose RA in its early stages. To find out if you have RA, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had RA.</li><li>Do a physical exam, which includes checking your joints, looking for rashes or nodules, and listening to your chest for signs of inflammation in your lungs.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies (x-ray or ultrasound) to make sure other health conditions aren't causing your symptoms since they may be like other types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> and joint conditions.</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> care) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>There is no cure for RA, but early treatment can help prevent your symptoms from getting worse and damaging your joints. Treatment can include medicine, lifestyle changes, and surgery. These may slow or stop joint damage and reduce pain and swelling.</p><p>Your provider may use a combination of treatments. Your treatment may change based on your symptoms.</p><p>You can help manage your RA symptoms if you:</p><ul><li>Are physically active</li><li>Keep a healthy weight</li><li>Avoid injuries to your joints</li><li>Avoid activities that have repetitive motions, like bending your knee over and over</li><li>Stop smoking, or don't start</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title">Juvenile <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>

      <content name="altTitle">Juvenile idiopathic <span class="qt0">arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> (JA) is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens in children. It causes joint inflammation (swelling), pain, stiffness, and loss of motion. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee. It can affect any joint, but it is more common in the knees, hands, and feet.</p><p>JA can affect your child's growth and development, and in some cases, it can also affect other organs. Finding JA early and starting treatment can help manage symptoms and reduce joint damage.</p>Who is more likely to get juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>There are several other forms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> affecting children. The most common type of JA in children under age 16 is juvenile idiopathic <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> (JIA). There are multiple types of JIA. Symptoms and the number of joints affected help determine the type. Some types of JIA are more common in girls.</p>What causes juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>The exact cause of JA is unknown. Most types are autoimmune disorders. This means that your immune system, which normally helps your body fight infection, attacks your body's tissues.</p>What are the symptoms of juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Symptoms can vary depending on the type of JA. The symptoms of most types include joint pain, swelling, warmth, and stiffness. Your child may not complain of pain or stiffness, but one early sign of JA may be limping or clumsiness in the morning or after resting. Larger joints, such as the knee, may be swollen.</p><p>Certain types of JA can cause a high fever, swollen lymph nodes, a rash, growth problems, or eye inflammation in some children. Symptoms can come and go. Some children have just one or two flare-ups. Others have symptoms that never go away.</p>How is juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> diagnosed?<p>There is no single test for JA, so it can be hard to diagnose. Your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about medical history and symptoms.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies.</li></ul>What are the treatments for juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>A team of providers usually treats JA. Treatment will depend on your child's age, the type of JA, and how bad it is. Treatment can include medicines and physical therapy to help maintain movement and reduce swelling and pain.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Arthritis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Joint inflammation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee.</p><p>Most types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> you have.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Common types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Osteoarthritis</span> is the most common type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>. It's often related to aging or injury.</li><li>Autoimmune <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake.  <span class="qt1">Rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is the most common form of this type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>.</li><li>Juvenile <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is a type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens in children.</li><li>Infectious <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> is one type.</li><li>Psoriatic <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches).</li><li>Gout is a painful type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected.</li><li>Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever, weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash.</p><p>Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> may be signs of other illnesses.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>A few things that might increase your chance of getting <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include:</p><ul><li>Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> if a member of your family has the disorder.</li><li>Age. The risk of getting many types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> increases with age.</li><li>Sex. Certain types of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> are more common in women, while other types are more common in men.</li></ul><p>Other factors that might increase your risk of getting <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> include having a previous joint injury, obesity, or lupus.</p>How is <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or take x-rays.</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> care) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>?<p>Treatment depends on the type of <span class="qt0">arthritis</span> you have. It may include medicine or surgery. Your provider will work with you to improve your symptoms and quality of life.</p><p>A few ways to help manage your symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Hot or cold packs</li><li>Relaxation techniques</li><li>Use of splints, braces, and/or assistive devices</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of <span class="qt0">Arthritis</span> and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/sjogrensdisease.html">
      <content name="title">Sjögren's Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sjögren's Syndrome</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is Sjögren's disease?<p>Sjögren's disease, previously called Sjögren's syndrome, is a chronic (long-lasting) autoimmune disease. When you have an autoimmune disease, your immune system attacks healthy tissues and organs by mistake. In Sjögren's disease, your immune system attacks the glands that make moisture in the eyes, mouth, and other parts of the body. This causes a dry mouth and dry eyes. You may have dryness in other places that need moisture, such as your nose, throat, and skin. Sjögren's disease can also affect other parts of the body, including your joints, lungs, kidneys, blood vessels, digestive organs, and nerves.</p>What causes Sjögren's disease?<p>Normally, your immune system protects the body from infection and disease. But with Sjögren's and other autoimmune diseases, your immune system attacks healthy tissues and organs. The cause of Sjögren's disease is unknown. Researchers think that genetic and environmental factors may play a role. Studies have linked Sjögren's disease to changes in several genes. Some researchers also think that the disease may be triggered by something in the environment. For example, they think that one possible trigger could be a previous infection with a virus or bacteria.</p>Who is more likely to develop Sjögren's disease?<p>Most people with Sjögren's disease are women. You can get it at any age, but it is most common in adults over age 50. It can affect people of any race or ethnicity.</p><p>Some people have Sjögren's disease on its own, while others have it with another autoimmune disease, such as <span class="qt1">rheumatoid</span> <span class="qt0">arthritis</span>, lupus or certain types of vasculitis. Because they have similar symptoms, having another autoimmune disease can sometimes make it harder to diagnose Sjögren's disease.</p>What are the symptoms of Sjögren's disease?<p>Sjögren's disease may have different effects on the body. Not everyone will have the same symptoms. Some people have cycles of mild and then severe symptoms.</p><p>The two main symptoms are:</p><ul><li>Dry eyes. Your eyes may burn or itch or feel like they have sand in them. Sometimes your vision may be blurry, or bright lights may bother you.</li><li>Dry mouth. Your tongue and your throat may feel dry. You might have trouble swallowing, speaking, and tasting.</li></ul><p>Sjögren's disease can also affect other parts of the body, causing symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Joint and muscle pain</li><li>Dry skin</li><li>Rashes on the skin of hands or feet</li><li>Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet</li><li>Acid reflux</li><li>Swelling in the glands around the face and neck</li><li>Trouble sleeping or concentrating</li><li>Vaginal dryness</li><li>Dry cough that doesn't go away</li><li>Fatigue that doesn't go away</li></ul><p>People with Sjögren's disease have a higher chance of getting lymphoma, but the risk is low.</p>How is Sjögren's disease diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for Sjögren's disease. To find out if you have it, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history and symptoms.</li><li>Will do a physical exam, which includes checking for signs of dry mouth and signs of related autoimmune diseases.</li><li>May order tests, including:
<ul><li>Eye tests to see if you produce a normal amount of tears and find out if your eyes have been damaged by dryness.</li><li>Salivary gland tests to measure how much saliva your mouth produces. They could include imaging tests and a biopsy.</li><li>Blood tests.</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for Sjögren's disease?<p>Treatment for Sjögren's disease focuses on relieving your symptoms and preventing any complications. The treatments can be different for each person, depending on which parts of the body are affected. They may include:</p><ul><li>Eye drops (artificial tears) or ointments to relieve dryness in the eyes.</li><li>Saliva substitutes.</li><li>Prescription medicines that cause your salivary glands to make more saliva.</li><li>A minor procedure that places small plugs in the tear ducts in the corners of your eyes. The plugs block your tears from draining so they stay in your eyes longer.</li><li>Medicines to help with other symptoms caused by Sjögren's disease, such as medicines for pain, inflammation, and mouth infections.</li><li>Medicines that suppress (weaken) your immune system (for severe cases).</li></ul><p>You can also try to relieve some of your symptoms by sucking on sugar-free candy, drinking water often, increasing the humidity in your room, and not smoking. Because having a dry mouth can raise your risk of cavities, it's important to take good care of your teeth and see your dentist regularly.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ankleinjuriesanddisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Ankle Injuries and Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your ankle bone and the ends of your two lower leg bones make up the ankle joint. Your ligaments, which connect bones to one another, stabilize and support it. Your muscles and tendons move it.</p><p>The most common ankle problems are sprains and fractures (broken bones). A sprain is an injury to the ligaments. It may take a few weeks to many months to heal completely.  A fracture is a break in a bone.  You can also injure other parts of the ankle such as tendons, which join muscles to bone, and cartilage, which cushions your joints. Ankle sprains and fractures are common sports injuries.</p></content>
